english: I'm here to get my Alien Registration Card issued
usage: I came to get my ARC issued
Polite; said at the counter to state your purpose
I came to get my ARC
반말, only if explaining to a friend, never to staff
I'm here to get my ARC, and…
Softer -는데요 ending that invites the clerk to guide you
I came to apply for foreigner registration
Focus on the application act (신청) rather than the card object
examples: 외국인등록증 발급받으러 왔어요.
I'm here to get my ARC issued.
The single opening line that tells staff exactly why you came
안녕하세요, 외국인등록증 발급받으러 왔는데요. 어디로 가면 돼요?
Hello, I'm here to get my ARC — where should I go?
Chain 어디로 가면 돼요 to ask which counter or floor
처음이라 외국인등록증 발급받으러 왔는데 뭐부터 해야 돼요?
It's my first time getting my ARC — what do I do first?
처음이라 ('since it's my first time') makes staff walk you through the steps
nuance: 외국인등록증 발급받으러 왔어요 is the core opening line at 출입국 (Immigration) or a service center: 외국인등록증 ('Alien Registration Card', the ARC every foreigner staying over 90 days must get) + 발급받다 ('to be issued / receive issuance') + -으러 왔어요 ('came in order to'). The card itself is 외국인등록증; Koreans say the full word 외국인등록증, but in everyday speech both applicants and staff routinely shorten it to 등록증. The grammar trap is the -으러 ending: it attaches to a verb stem to mean 'in order to do', so it must ride on 받으러 (the verb), NOT on the noun — saying 외국인등록증으로 왔어요 ('I came BY means of the ARC') is a real beginner slip caused by confusing -으러 ('in order to') with -으로 ('by/with'). Register is plain 존댓말 (-어요), which is exactly right for a government counter: not stiff 합쇼체, not casual 반말. A near-synonym is 외국인등록 신청하러 왔어요 ('I came to APPLY for registration') — use 신청하러 when you're starting the paperwork and 발급받으러 when the focus is walking out with the physical card. The English-speaker pitfall is 직역: translating 'I want to register' as 등록하고 싶어요, which sounds like a vague wish; at a counter you state the purpose with -으러 왔어요, not a desire with -고 싶어요. Also note 발급받다 (you receive) vs 발급하다 (the office issues) — you, the applicant, 발급받다.

english: I'd like to extend my stay
usage: I'd like to extend my period of stay
Polite; the standard way to state the visit's purpose
I came to extend my stay
States it as the reason you're physically here
I'm here to extend my stay, and…
Short everyday form with the soft -는데요 lead-in
I'd like to extend my visa
Everyday phrasing — many say 비자 연장 for 체류 연장
examples: 체류 기간 연장하고 싶어요.
I'd like to extend my period of stay.
A clear one-line purpose statement at the counter
저 다음 달에 비자 끝나서 체류 기간 연장하려고 왔어요.
My visa ends next month, so I came to extend my stay.
Give the reason with -서 ('because') before the request
체류 연장하려면 어떤 서류가 필요해요?
What documents do I need to extend my stay?
-려면 ('if I want to') asks what's required for the extension
nuance: 체류 기간 연장 is the official term for extending your authorized stay: 체류 ('staying/residence', Sino-Korean 滯留) + 기간 ('period') + 연장 ('extension', 延長). On forms and signs you'll see 체류기간 연장허가 ('permission to extend period of stay'), so 체류 기간 연장 is the phrase that matches the bureaucracy. In everyday speech many foreigners and even staff say 비자 연장 ('visa extension'), and that's understood — but technically you extend your 체류 기간 (the stay tied to your status), and the 비자 (the entry sticker) is a slightly different thing; for talking to officials, 체류 기간 연장 is the precise term. The dividing line: use -하고 싶어요 ('I'd like to') to state the goal politely, or -하러/하려고 왔어요 ('I came in order to') to frame it as why you're here — both are natural; officials respond to either. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 of 'renew': learners reach for 갱신, but 갱신 (renewal) is mostly for re-issuing an expiring card/ARC, while 연장 (extension) is for adding more time to your stay — picking the wrong one confuses the clerk about which service you want. Register is plain 존댓말, perfect for a counter. Don't drop 기간 awkwardly mid-sentence; 체류 연장 (without 기간) is the accepted short form, but 체류만 연장 sounds incomplete.

연장 adds time to your stay; 갱신 re-issues an expiring document. To stay longer, say 체류 기간 연장; to replace an expiring ARC, say 갱신.
Saying 체류를 늘리고 싶어요.
늘리다 ('to increase/lengthen') is too literal/physical here. The fixed bureaucratic verb is 연장하다: 체류 기간 연장하고 싶어요.
Treating 비자 and 체류 기간 as identical to an official.
Casually 비자 연장 is fine, but precisely you extend 체류 기간 (your stay). For accuracy with staff, say 체류 기간 연장.

english: What type of visa is it?
usage: Polite-neutral; asking which visa category applies
Asking specifically about your own visa status
May I ask your visa type?
Honorific 어떻게 되세요 — what STAFF say to you
examples: 제 비자 종류가 뭐예요?
What type is my visa?
Asking the clerk to confirm your category
이 일 하려면 비자 종류가 뭐예요? 바꿔야 돼요?
What visa type do I need for this job — do I have to change it?
Link to 바꿔야 돼요 to ask about changing status
비자 종류가 어떻게 되세요? — E-7이요.
May I ask your visa type? — It's E-7.
How staff ask, and how you answer with the code
nuance: 비자 종류가 뭐예요? is 비자 ('visa') + 종류 ('type/kind', 種類) + 가 뭐예요 ('what is'), used to ask or confirm which visa category (D-2 student, E-2 teaching, E-7 work, F-6 marriage, etc.) is in play. Knowing your 종류 matters because every service — 연장, 변경, 신고 — depends on it. The key register split is who asks: a clerk will ask you honorifically, 비자 종류가 어떻게 되세요? (어떻게 되세요 is the polite 'how is it / may I ask'), and you answer plainly with the code, 'E-7이요'. If YOU ask, the neutral 비자 종류가 뭐예요? or casual 무슨 비자예요? is right — but never answer a clerk's honorific question by bouncing 어떻게 되세요 back at yourself. The near-synonym 비자 상태 ('visa status') sounds like English 'status' but in Korean offices the operative word is 종류 (category) or 체류자격 ('status of stay', the formal term on documents); if you want to sound official, 체류자격이 어떻게 되세요? is what appears on forms. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 of 'what is my visa status' as 제 비자 상태가 뭐예요?, which Koreans parse as 'is my visa okay/valid?' rather than 'which category'; to ask the category, say 종류 or 체류자격. Particle note: it's 종류'가' 뭐예요 (subject 가), not 종류'를'.

어떻게 되세요 is honorific, aimed AT you. You answer plainly: just state the code, 'F-6이요', not by re-asking 어떻게 돼요.
Saying 비자 상태가 뭐예요 to mean 'which category'.
상태 ('state/condition') sounds like asking if it's valid. For the category, say 비자 종류가 뭐예요 or the formal 체류자격.
Using 를 instead of 가: 비자 종류를 뭐예요.
'What is X' takes the subject particle: 비자 종류가 뭐예요. 를 marks an object and is ungrammatical with 뭐예요.

english: How do I fill out the application form?
usage: How do I fill out the application form?
Polite; asking staff to guide you through the form
How do I write the application?
Everyday 쓰다 instead of formal 작성하다
Please show me how to fill this out
-는지 알려 주세요 asks them to teach you the how
Pointing at one blank field on the form
examples: 이 신청서 어떻게 작성해요?
How do I fill out this application form?
Holding up the blank form to ask for help
여기 영어로 작성해도 돼요?
Can I fill this out in English?
-도 돼요 asks if English is acceptable on the form
이 칸은 뭘 적는지 몰라서요, 어떻게 작성해요?
I don't know what goes in this box — how do I fill it in?
칸 ('box/field') + -는지 몰라서 explains your confusion politely
nuance: 신청서 어떻게 작성해요? is 신청서 ('application form', 申請書) + 어떻게 ('how') + 작성하다 ('to fill out / draw up', 作成), the line that gets a clerk to walk you through the paperwork. 작성하다 is the proper, slightly formal verb for completing a form or document; in casual speech you'd say 쓰다 ('write') or 적다 ('jot/note'), and 어떻게 써요? is perfectly natural and a bit warmer. The dividing line: 작성하다 is for filling out a whole document (form, report), while 적다/쓰다 fit a single field — so 'how do I fill out the form' is 작성, but 'what do I write in this box' is 여기 뭐 적어요?. The near-synonym 기입하다 ('to enter/inscribe') also means filling in fields and shows up on official instructions, but it sounds bookish to say aloud; stick with 작성/적다 when speaking. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 of 'fill out' as 채우다 ('to fill (a container)') — 신청서를 채워요 sounds like physically stuffing the form full, not completing it; the right verb is 작성하다. Register stays plain 존댓말. Particle-wise you can drop the object marker in speech (신청서 작성해요 rather than 신청서를), which is natural and common. Pair it with 영어로 작성해도 돼요? to check if you may write in English, a very common real concern.

채우다 means filling a container (a cup, a tank). Completing a form uses 작성하다: 신청서 어떻게 작성해요?
Using 작성하다 for one tiny field.
작성 is for a whole document. For a single box ask 여기 뭐 적어요? or 뭐 써요? — 적다/쓰다 fit individual fields better.
Confusing 신청서 (application form) with 신청 (the act of applying).
신청서 is the paper; 신청 is applying. 'How do I fill out the FORM' needs 신청서: 신청서 어떻게 작성해요?

usage: Polite; asking where to hand in your paperwork
-면 돼요 ('where is fine to') sounds a touch softer
Casual word order, common in quick speech
접수되다 (passive) checks if this counter takes it
examples: 이거 어디에서 접수해요?
Where do I submit this?
Holding your documents, asking which counter takes them
서류 다 썼는데 어디에서 접수하면 돼요?
I've finished the forms — where do I submit them?
다 썼는데 ('I've finished and…') leads into the where question
여기서 접수하고 번호표 뽑으면 돼요?
Do I submit here and then take a number ticket?
Link 접수 with 번호표 뽑다 ('take a queue ticket')
nuance: 어디에서 접수해요? is 어디에서 ('at where') + 접수하다 ('to submit / receive intake', 接受). 접수 is the bureaucratic word for the intake of documents — handing in your application so it's officially received and processed. It cuts both ways: as the applicant you 접수하다 (submit), and the office 접수받다/접수하다 (receives) it; the counter where this happens is the 접수처 or 접수 창구. The subtle point English speakers miss is that 접수 is NOT just 'submit a paper' — it means lodging it into the system so it's logged, so 'I submitted my application and got a receipt number' is all 접수. The near-synonym 제출하다 ('to submit/turn in', 提出) overlaps but leans toward handing over a specific document (a report, a certificate), while 접수 emphasizes the office accepting and registering your case — at immigration, 접수 is the word on the signs and tickets. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 of 'submit' always as 제출, then being confused by 접수 on every sign; learn 접수 as the front-desk intake verb. The passive 접수되다 ('to be accepted/received') is handy to ask 이거 접수돼요? ('will this be accepted?').

접수 is the office formally receiving and logging your case. It covers submitting, getting a number, and being entered into the system — broader than 제출.
Mixing up 접수 (intake) and 영수증 (receipt).

usage: I booked a visit and came
Polite; telling staff you have an online appointment
I have a reservation — where do I go?
Soft -는데요 lead-in then asks the way
I came without a reservation — can I still be seen?
Checks walk-in acceptance when you have no booking
How do I make a reservation?
Asking how to book if you haven't yet
examples: 오늘 2시로 방문 예약하고 왔어요.
I booked a 2 o'clock visit for today.
Give the time slot with -로 ('for') to confirm your booking
하이코리아에서 예약했는데요, 여기 맞아요?
I booked on HiKorea — is this the right place?
하이코리아 ('HiKorea') is the official booking site
예약 안 하면 오래 기다려요? 예약하고 오는 게 나아요?
Is the wait long without a reservation? Is it better to book first?
Compares walk-in vs booking with -는 게 나아요 ('is better')

The -하고 왔어요 structure ('I did X and came') is the natural way to report a completed precondition: you booked, then showed up. The key vocabulary point is 예약 ('reservation/booking', for a future slot — restaurants, hospitals, offices) — don't confuse it with 약속 ('a promise / a personal appointment to meet someone'); saying 약속하고 왔어요 would mean 'I made a personal promise and came', which baffles a clerk. The dividing line: 설명하다 ('explain', lay out how something works) vs 말하다 ('say/tell') vs 알려 주다 ('let me know/inform') — for 'walk me through this again' it's 설명, while 'tell me one more time' is 다시 말씀해 주세요. The honorific 말씀하다 (humble/honorific 'to speak') is what you use for the staff's speaking: 다시 한번 말씀해 주세요.

The request ending -아/어 주시겠어요? layers 주다 ('do for me, as a favor') + -시- (honorific) + -겠어요 (softening conditional) + question, making it the gentlest, most deferential way to ask someone to do something — far softer than the plain 설명해 주세요 ('please explain') and miles from the bare imperative 설명하세요 ('explain!'), which sounds like ordering staff around.

The register mismatch of using flat imperatives (설명해, 말해) with officials, or the 직역 of 'one more time' that omits the honorific. Also 'I don't understand' is best as 이해가 잘 안 돼요 (이해가 안 되다, 'understanding doesn't happen', with 이해'가' as subject), not the 직역 제가 이해 안 해요 ('I don't do understanding'), which is wrong because 이해되다 is the natural passive.

mistakes: Saying 설명하세요 or 설명해 to staff.
Bare imperatives sound like ordering them. Use the polite request: 다시 설명해 주시겠어요? or at least 설명해 주세요.
Saying 제가 이해 안 해요 for 'I don't understand'.
이해되다 is the natural form: 이해가 안 돼요 / 이해가 잘 안 돼요. 이해 안 해요 ('I don't do understanding') is unnatural.
Using 설명 when you mean the meaning of a word.
설명 is 'explain how it works'. For 'what does this word mean', ask 이게 무슨 뜻이에요? — 뜻 ('meaning') fits a single term.

Plain-language version of the same worry
Does my status stay the same?
Asks if your status survives the trip

nuance: 재입국 허가 받아야 돼요? is 재입국 ('re-entry', 再入國) + 허가 ('permit/permission', 許可) + 받다 ('to receive') + -아야 돼요? ('do I have to…?'), the essential question before leaving Korea temporarily so your residence status survives the trip. 재입국 허가 (re-entry permit) is the formal term; many statuses are now exempt for short trips, which is exactly why you ask whether you 받아야 돼요 ('have to get one'). The verb pairing is the lesson again: you 허가를 받다 ('receive a permit'), while the government 허가를 내주다/허가하다 ('grants/issues' it) — so it's 허가 받아야 돼요 (you receive), never 허가 해야 돼요 (which sounds like YOU grant the permit). The English-speaker pitfall: the 직역 of 'permit' as 퍼밋 or as 허락; 허락 ('permission/consent') is the everyday word for personal permission (parents 허락, a boss's 허락), whereas the official governmental authorization is 허가 — at immigration it's 허가. The dividing line in plain speech: 재입국 허가 받아야 돼요? (formal) vs 출국했다가 다시 들어와도 돼요? ('can I leave and re-enter?', 들어오다 = 'come in') — both work, the first matching the bureaucratic term. Useful is the 안 ~아도 돼요 frame for exemptions: 재입국 허가 안 받아도 돼요? ('is it okay NOT to get one?'). Register plain 존댓말. Note 출국 ('leaving the country') vs 입국 ('entering') vs 재입국 ('re-entering') as a clean trio worth learning together.
